# Start Using Microsoft Copilot in Word, Excel, and Outlook

Imagine having a helpful, incredibly fast assistant sitting right inside your everyday office apps, ready to write drafts, crunch numbers, and clear out your inbox. This guide will show you how to start using Microsoft Copilot to save time and reduce office stress today. While Copilot can draft text, analyze data, or summarize emails, remember it's an **AI assistant** — you'll still need to review, edit, and send your work, as it cannot perform actions like sending emails or saving files on its own.

## Before you start
- You need a **Microsoft 365 plan or license that includes Copilot** (for example a personal or family plan that includes Copilot, or a work or school account where your organization has assigned you a Copilot license). Plan names change from time to time, so check your Microsoft account page or ask your IT admin what yours includes.
- Access to **Microsoft Word, Excel, and Outlook**, either the desktop versions installed on your computer or through a web browser. Ensure you're logged into your Microsoft 365 account.
- A **stable internet connection** is essential, as Copilot relies on cloud-based AI to process your requests.
- Allow about **15-20 minutes** to follow along with these steps across the different applications.

## Step 1 — Start a draft in Word
Open Microsoft Word and begin a new, blank document. Look for the Copilot option: Microsoft's help page describes a Copilot prompt box near the bottom of the document window, and there can also be a Copilot button on the ribbon at the top. Select it to open Copilot. This is where you'll type your instructions, known as **prompts** (which is simply the plain-language command you give to the AI assistant, just as if you were speaking to a colleague).

If it looks different: The exact place and look of the Copilot option differ between Word versions, the web version, and plans. Look for something that clearly says "Copilot". If you don't see it, check that your plan includes Copilot and that Word is updated.
You'll know it worked when: A box or side panel appears where you can type your request.

💬 Example:
> In the Copilot box, type:
> "Write a three-paragraph project proposal for a new staff wellness initiative, including a suggested timeline and a bulleted list of benefits."

## Step 2 — Generate and refine your Word draft
Once you've typed your prompt into the Copilot box, send it (press Enter or select the send or generate option next to the box). Copilot will then process your request and write a draft for you. When the draft appears, you will usually be able to keep it, discard it, or ask for another version. You can also give further instructions to refine the draft. For instance, you might ask it to change the tone or expand on a specific section.

If it looks different: The names of the options differ between versions. If the generated text isn't quite right, don't worry – simply type a new, more specific instruction to guide it further.
You'll know it worked when: A draft appears in your document, and you can accept it, discard it, or type more instructions to refine it.

💬 Example:
> After Copilot generates the proposal, type:
> "Make the tone of the proposal more formal and add a section about potential budget considerations."

## Step 3 — Prepare your data in Excel for analysis
Open a spreadsheet in Microsoft Excel that contains data you want to analyze. Copilot works best when your data is organized as an Excel **Table**. Think of a Table as neatly labeled boxes for your data — it helps Excel (and Copilot) know exactly where your information starts and ends, and what each column represents. To convert your data, first select all the cells that contain your information (including the column headers). Then use the Format as Table option on the Home tab, or press `Ctrl + T` (Windows) or `Cmd + T` (Mac). If your first row contains titles for each column, make sure the option saying your table has headers is ticked.

If it looks different: The names and places of these options can differ between Excel versions and the web version. If Copilot says it can't work with your data, check that the data has clear column headers and no empty rows or columns in the middle.
You'll know it worked when: Your data is shown as a structured Table, with a header row and small filter arrows on the headers.

## Step 4 — Analyze your Excel data with Copilot
With your data organized as an Excel Table, it's ready for Copilot. Look for the Copilot icon in the lower-right area of the Excel window (the exact place can differ between versions). Select it to open Copilot. Once it's open, you can ask Copilot specific questions or give it instructions about your data. Copilot acts like a friendly data coach, helping with analysis by processing numbers, offering insights, or suggesting visual changes to your spreadsheet (such as charts or formatting).

If it looks different: If you can't find Copilot, check that your Excel version is up to date and that your plan includes Copilot, then try restarting Excel.
You'll know it worked when: A Copilot panel appears, ready for your input, and it may offer a few starter suggestions based on your data.

💬 Example:
> In the Excel Copilot panel, type:
> "Show me the total sales for each region and suggest charts to visualize the top three performing products."

## Step 5 — Summarize an email thread in Outlook
Returning to a massive chain of emails can be daunting. Luckily, Copilot can summarize long email threads in Outlook, saving you from reading every single reply. To use this, open the email thread you want to summarize by selecting it in your inbox. In a long enough conversation, look at the top of the thread for a **Summary by Copilot** or **Summarize** option. Select it, and Copilot will go through the conversation and pull out the most important information.

If it looks different: The label can differ between Outlook versions. The option appears for longer conversations, so if you don't see it, make sure you're viewing a thread, not a single short message, and that your plan includes Copilot.
You'll know it worked when: A short summary appears at the top of the thread, outlining the main points of the conversation.

💬 Example:
> Open a long email thread, then select the **Summarize** option (or Summary by Copilot) at the top.

## Step 6 — Draft quick email replies in Outlook
Instead of staring at a blank reply box trying to find the right words, you can let Copilot help you draft your response. Open an email and start a reply. In the reply window, look for a Copilot option, if your Outlook version and plan offer one. Select it and tell Copilot what kind of reply you need. Copilot will draft an email based on your instructions and the context of the original message. You stay in charge: read the draft, adjust it, and send it only when you are happy with it.

If it looks different: The place and the name of the Copilot option in the reply window differ between Outlook versions, and it may not be available in every version or plan. If you can't find it, you can still ask Copilot for help in its chat and paste the text into your reply.
You'll know it worked when: A draft reply appears, ready for your review and any final edits.

💬 Example:
> When replying to an email, ask Copilot:
> "Reply to Sarah. Agree to the meeting on Tuesday at 10:00am, but ask if we can keep it to 30 minutes because of another commitment."

## Common mistakes
-   **Expecting perfect accuracy (hallucinations):** Copilot, like all AI, can sometimes make mistakes or confidently present incorrect facts or numbers, a phenomenon often called **hallucinations** (where the AI makes things up).
    -   **Fix:** Always double-check important dates, figures, names, and critical information before sending or saving any work generated by Copilot. Treat its output as a helpful first draft, not a final version.
-   **Using loose Excel data:** If your spreadsheet is a jumble of raw numbers with no clear headers, Copilot may struggle to understand your data or your query.
    -   **Fix:** Take a minute to give every column a clear header and, ideally, turn the data into a Table (see Step 3) *before* trying to use Copilot in Excel. This gives Copilot the structured data it needs.
-   **Being too brief with prompts:** If you type a vague instruction like "write a report," Copilot has to guess what you want, often leading to generic results that don't quite fit your needs.
    -   **Fix:** The more specific and detailed your **prompt** (e.g., target audience, length, tone, specific points to include), the better and more relevant your first draft will be. Tell it exactly what you're hoping for.

## What this means for you
-   **In everyday life:** You can use these same skills for personal tasks. Draft a polite letter to your landlord, create a summary of a long family email chain, or organize your household budget data more effectively. Copilot helps with tasks big and small.
-   **For your business or work:** Copilot streamlines daily tasks, freeing up valuable time. Imagine quickly drafting meeting agendas, summarizing customer feedback emails, or analyzing sales figures without spending hours on data entry or initial writing. It can boost productivity across your team.
-   **If you're just getting started:** Pick one app you use most often, like Word or Outlook, and try one simple Copilot feature, like drafting an email or generating a short document. Start small to build confidence and see the benefits firsthand.

## Try it now
Open Microsoft Word, create a new document, and open Copilot. In the box, type: "Write a short thank you note for a team member who helped me with a difficult project." See what it generates!
